q:
Consider the following statements:
1. No charge can be booked under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense unless a work order covering the job has been issued.
2. The issue of a work order presupposes a sanctioned estimate or an authorised programme or indent.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Workshop Manufacturing Suspense can be debited only under an issued work order, and a work order itself presupposes a sanctioned estimate, authorised programme or indent, so both statements state the basic control in workshop accounts.

q: For one particular identified manufacture job, the shop is given a work order that will be closed when that job is done, instead of a work order covering its routine repetitive work. Such a work order is a:

options.A: Specific (shop) work order
options.B: Revenue standing work order
options.C: On-cost standing work order
options.D: Batch work order for stock manufacture

e: A work order opened for one particular identified job and closed on its completion is a specific shop work order, unlike a standing order which covers routine repetitive work over a period.

q: Components are made in a workshop in lots, not against any single indent, but for being stocked in the stores depot. The class of work order under which such lot manufacture is carried out is the:

options.A: Revenue standing work order
options.B: Verbal instruction of the shop incharge
options.C: Material requisition, without any work order
options.D: Batch work order, the cost being accumulated for the batch as a whole

e: Manufacture in lots for stock, with cost accumulated for the whole batch rather than against a single indent, is executed under a batch work order for stock manufacture in the stores depot.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Proforma charges are levied on workshop jobs so that the cost of the outturn can be compared with trade or market prices.
2. Proforma charges involve an actual cash payment by the workshop.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Proforma charges are notional charges included only to make workshop cost comparable with trade or market prices. They involve no actual cash payment, so statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is not.

q: Which of the following groups of expenses together make up the general on-cost of a workshop?

options.A: Raw material issued to all the shops
options.B: Direct labour charges of the workshop
options.C: Bonus paid under the incentive scheme
options.D: Indirect expenses that are common to the workshop as a whole, like general administration and general supervision

e: General on-cost consists of indirect expenses common to the workshop as a whole, such as general administration and general supervision, which cannot be tied to one shop or one job.

q: The Workshop Accounts Officer advises that on-cost be absorbed shop by shop instead of at one common rate for the whole workshop. His reason is that:

options.A: A common rate can be applied only to capital jobs
options.B: The indirect expenses of the several shops differ widely, so a common rate would load some jobs with too much on-cost and others with too little
options.C: Shops are not permitted to maintain their own on-cost accounts
options.D: A common rate can be applied only in production units

e: Shop-wise absorption is preferred because indirect expenses differ widely between shops. A single common rate would overcharge jobs of a low-cost shop and undercharge jobs of a high-cost shop.

q: A group turns out a quantity of work in a period, but a part of it is rejected at inspection. Under the Group Incentive Scheme, the incentive of the group is reckoned on:

options.A: All the outturn turned out, including the rejected portion
options.B: The attendance of the members of the group alone
options.C: Only the outturn that has been passed and accepted, the rejected portion being excluded
options.D: Savings in material cost alone

e: Under the Group Incentive Scheme bonus is reckoned only on outturn passed and accepted at inspection. Rejected work earns no incentive, as payment is for acceptable production only.

q: Before a period begins, a target is set for a group working under the Group Incentive Scheme. This target is worked out mainly from:

options.A: The sanctioned strength of the group and the allowed-time norms for the units it has to turn out
options.B: The total earnings of the workshop in the previous year
options.C: The number of machines installed in the shop
options.D: The outturn of the best-performing group of the workshop

e: The group target is set from the sanctioned strength of the group and the allowed-time norms for the units to be turned out, linking the target to manpower and measured work content.

q: At the end of a period, the accepted outturn of a group is found to be below the target set under the Group Incentive Scheme. The result for the group is that:

options.A: It still receives the full bonus at the target rate
options.B: Its members are fined an amount equal to the value of the shortfall
options.C: The shortfall is ignored and the same target bonus is paid
options.D: Its incentive is reduced in proportion to the shortfall, and if the outturn falls below the prescribed minimum level, no incentive is payable at all

e: If accepted outturn falls short of target, incentive is reduced proportionately to the shortfall. Below the prescribed minimum level of outturn, no incentive is payable at all.

q: As distinct from the individual incentive scheme, the Group Incentive Scheme is mainly found working in:

options.A: Stores depots of the railway
options.B: Repair workshops engaged on Periodic Overhaul and repairs of rolling stock
options.C: Production units manufacturing new locomotives
options.D: Railway printing presses only

e: The Group Incentive Scheme works mainly in repair workshops doing Periodic Overhaul and repairs of rolling stock, where outturn is by groups or gangs rather than by individual measured jobs.

q: For measuring outturn under the Group Incentive Scheme, the 'group' is ordinarily made up of:

options.A: All the workshops of the railway taken together
options.B: Only the supervisory staff of the shop
options.C: The workers of a shop or a section, together with the essential indirect workers attached to that shop or section
options.D: Only the apprentices undergoing training in the shop

e: For group incentive, the group ordinarily comprises the workers of a shop or section together with the essential indirect workers attached to that shop or section who support its outturn.

q: The letters 'CLW' in the CLW pattern of incentive scheme stand for the works at which that pattern originated, namely:

options.A: Central Labour Workshop
options.B: Chittaranjan Locomotive Works
options.C: Carriage and Locomotive Workshop, Perambur
options.D: Central Locomotive Works, Varanasi

e: CLW stands for Chittaranjan Locomotive Works, where the CLW pattern of incentive scheme originated and from which the pattern takes its name.

q: A worker working under the CLW pattern finishes a job in less than the time allowed for it. His bonus for the job is reckoned on:

options.A: 50 per cent of the value of the time he has saved
options.B: 30 per cent of the value of the time he has saved
options.C: The time actually taken by him only, with no bonus at all
options.D: The full value of the time he has saved, his earnings being worked out on the allowed time for the job

e: Under the CLW pattern the worker is paid on the allowed time for the job, so he gets the full value of the time saved, unlike patterns that share the saving only in part.

q: Before a job is put on the incentive scheme, the rate fixer first determines how long it should take. He does this on the basis of:

options.A: Time studies, that is, work measurement, carried out for the purpose
options.B: Negotiation with the recognised union
options.C: A rough estimate made by the shop incharge
options.D: The actual time taken on the job in the previous year

e: Allowed time is set by the rate fixer on the basis of time studies and work measurement, not by negotiation, rough estimate or last year's actual time.

q: A worker completes a job in less time than was allowed for it. The 'time saved' by him, in incentive terminology, is arrived at by:

options.A: Deducting the allowed time from the time actually taken
options.B: Deducting the idle time from the hours of attendance
options.C: Deducting the time actually taken from the allowed time for the job
options.D: Deducting the leave availed of by him from the allowed time

e: Time saved is the excess of allowed time over time actually taken for the job. It is allowed time minus actual time taken, as per standard incentive terminology.

q: The allowed time fixed for a job under work measurement is built up as:

options.A: The time taken by the fastest worker in the shop on that job
options.B: The normal time for the job, with the prescribed allowances such as fatigue or relaxation allowance added to it
options.C: The time taken on the same job in the previous year
options.D: A time fixed by negotiation with the staff side

e: Allowed time is built up from the normal time for the job plus prescribed allowances, such as fatigue or relaxation allowance, as determined by work measurement.

q: A shop incharge proposes paying incentive bonus on every job done in his shop. Under the scheme, bonus can in fact be paid only on:

options.A: All jobs done in the workshop, whether measured or not
options.B: Jobs done by indirect workers of the shop
options.C: Jobs done on standing work orders only
options.D: Jobs that have been measured and for which allowed times have been fixed

e: Incentive bonus is payable only on measured jobs for which allowed times have been fixed. Unmeasured work has no time saving to measure, so no bonus can be computed on it.

q: Which of the following categories of workshop staff remain outside the incentive scheme?

options.A: Direct workers engaged on measured jobs
options.B: Essential indirect workers attached to the shops
options.C: General indirect and office (clerical) staff who are not connected with production
options.D: Gang workers sharing the bonus of their group

e: General indirect and office or clerical staff not connected with production remain outside the incentive scheme, which covers direct workers and essential indirect workers attached to shops.

q: In the language of work measurement, a 'standard hour' means:

options.A: The quantity of work that a qualified worker can turn out in one hour when working at standard performance
options.B: The clock hour in which the maximum work is done in a shop
options.C: The hour of attendance recorded on the gate card
options.D: An overtime hour paid at double the normal rate

e: A standard hour is the quantity of work a qualified worker can turn out in one hour at standard performance. It is a unit of work content, not a clock hour of attendance.

q: A chargeman wants his men to stay back beyond normal hours to finish urgent work. Overtime in the workshop can be worked:

options.A: Whenever the chargeman considers it necessary, without any sanction
options.B: Only on days when the workshop remains closed
options.C: Only by casual labour engaged for the purpose
options.D: Only after the prior sanction of the competent authority has been obtained

e: Overtime in a workshop requires prior sanction of the competent authority. A chargeman or shop incharge cannot authorise overtime on his own whenever he considers it necessary.

q: For the hours a workshop worker works beyond nine hours in a day, or beyond forty-eight hours in a week, the Factories Act, 1948 entitles him to wages at:

options.A: The ordinary rate of wages
options.B: Twice the ordinary rate of wages
options.C: One and a half times the ordinary rate of wages
options.D: Three times the ordinary rate of wages

e: Section 59 of the Factories Act, 1948 provides wages at twice the ordinary rate for work beyond nine hours a day or beyond forty-eight hours a week.

q: Sitting at the workshop gate, the time keeper makes up the time book of the workshop. The record from which he makes it up is:

options.A: The labour pay sheets of the workshop
options.B: The route cards of the jobs in progress
options.C: The gate attendance (clock) cards of the workers
options.D: The stores issue notes of the depot

e: The time keeper prepares the time book from the gate attendance or clock cards of workers, which record actual arrival and departure at the workshop gate.

q: Where a shop works on payment by results, the quantity on which a worker's pay is worked out is taken from:

options.A: The piece-work tickets, which show the quantity produced by him and passed as accepted after inspection
options.B: The gate attendance cards of the worker
options.C: The material requisitions issued to the shop
options.D: The completion report of the last job of the shop

e: Where payment is by results, pay is based on piece-work tickets showing the quantity produced by the worker and passed as accepted after inspection, not on attendance alone.

q: A new machine is received and installed in a workshop. Its cost and particulars, under a distinctive number allotted to that machine, are entered in:

options.A: The Workshop General Register
options.B: The stores price ledger
options.C: The Plant Register of the workshop
options.D: The completion report book

e: A new machine is entered, under a distinctive number allotted to it, in the Plant Register of the workshop, which records its cost and particulars for maintenance and accountal.

q: The upkeep of a workshop machine is handed over to an outside agency under a maintenance contract. The payments made to the agency under the contract are booked in the same way as the cost of:

options.A: A manufacture job for the stores depot
options.B: Repairs and maintenance of that machine, under the standing arrangement that covers machinery repairs
options.C: New machinery under the Machinery and Plant Programme
options.D: Incentive bonus of the maintenance staff

e: Payments under an outside maintenance contract for a machine are booked like the cost of repairs and maintenance of that machine, under the standing arrangement covering machinery repairs.

q: The money for buying new machinery and plant for a workshop is found, not from Workshop Manufacturing Suspense, but through:

options.A: Shop on-cost of the workshop
options.B: Revenue standing work orders
options.C: The unpaid wages head of the workshop
options.D: The Machinery and Plant Programme, the charge falling on Capital or the Depreciation Reserve Fund as applicable

e: New machinery and plant is financed through the Machinery and Plant Programme, with the charge falling on Capital or the Depreciation Reserve Fund as applicable, not through Workshop Manufacturing Suspense.

q: The stores depot issues material against a manufacture job of a workshop. The first accounting entry for this issue debits:

options.A: Workshop Manufacturing Suspense, under the work order of that job
options.B: The final Revenue head of the job
options.C: The Stock Adjustment Account
options.D: The shop on-cost account directly

e: Material issued by the stores depot against a manufacture job is first debited to Workshop Manufacturing Suspense under the work order of that job, for later transfer to the final head.

q: For collecting the cost of work done and keeping control over it, every shop or section of a workshop is reckoned as a:

options.A: Profit centre
options.B: Cost centre
options.C: Stores depot
options.D: Separate accounting unit rendering its own Account Current

e: Each shop or section is treated as a cost centre for collecting the cost of work done and exercising control over it, with its labour, material and on-cost accumulated separately.

q: The follow-up, or progress, work of production control in a workshop consists of:

options.A: Preparing the annual budget of the workshop
options.B: Inspecting the finished articles for quality
options.C: Maintaining the gate attendance cards of staff
options.D: Chasing and expediting jobs and materials through the successive shops so that the programme is not held up

e: Progress or follow-up in production control means chasing and expediting jobs and materials through successive shops so that the production programme is not held up.

q: Which of the following is a proforma on-cost item of a workshop?

options.A: Wages of direct shop staff engaged on jobs
options.B: Cost of raw material issued to jobs
options.C: Provident Fund contribution, together with depreciation of workshop plant and buildings
options.D: Power consumed by shop machines

e: Proforma on-cost is a notional element covering Provident Fund contribution and depreciation of workshop plant and buildings, added to make workshop cost comparable with trade cost.

q: At the end of a month several manufacture and repair jobs in a workshop are still incomplete. The debit balance standing under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense at that stage represents:

options.A: The value of labour, material and on-cost booked on jobs in progress in the workshop
options.B: The book value of machinery and plant installed in the workshop
options.C: The value of finished articles held in the stores depot
options.D: The arrears of wages payable to workshop staff

e: The debit balance under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense at month-end represents labour, material and on-cost booked on jobs still in progress, that is, work-in-progress of the workshop.

q: A workshop has to spread its indirect expenses over the jobs executed during a period. In workshop accounts this distribution of on-cost over jobs is generally made on the basis of:

options.A: The cost of material consumed on each job
options.B: The direct labour charges booked on each job
options.C: The floor area occupied by each job in the shop
options.D: The number of machines installed in the shop

e: On-cost is generally distributed over jobs on the basis of direct labour charges booked on each job, as indirect expenses are most closely related to labour employed.

q: While compiling the full cost of a manufactured article, the Accounts office adds a notional element described as proforma on-cost. That element covers:

options.A: The wages of direct workers engaged on the article
options.B: The cost of raw material issued for the article
options.C: Provident Fund contribution and depreciation of workshop plant and buildings
options.D: Electric power consumed by the machines on that job

e: Proforma on-cost added during cost compilation covers notional items like Provident Fund contribution and depreciation of workshop plant and buildings, not direct wages, material or power.

q: After the labour pay sheets of a workshop are prepared, a difference is noticed between the total of the time and tally sheets and the total of the pay sheets. In workshop accounts this difference is ordinarily charged to:

options.A: A capital work order of the workshop
options.B: The work order of the largest job in hand
options.C: General on-cost of the workshop
options.D: Shop on-cost

e: A difference between the totals of time and tally sheets and the labour pay sheets, which cannot be tied to a job, is charged to shop on-cost as per workshop accounts practice.

q: A chargeman points out that a particular work order for routine repair work chargeable to revenue is used year after year without a fresh order being issued. Such an order is a revenue standing work order, characterised by the fact that it:

options.A: Remains unchanged from year to year for routine revenue jobs
options.B: Is sanctioned afresh by the Railway Board for every job
options.C: Is issued separately for every single repair undertaken
options.D: Cannot be used for any repair work at all

e: A revenue standing work order covers routine repair work chargeable to revenue and remains unchanged from year to year, without a fresh order for every job.

q: A shop is asked to show the document on the authority of which manufacture of an article was undertaken in the workshop. The document to be produced for this purpose is the:

options.A: Gate pass issued for taking material out of the workshop
options.B: Route card for the manufacture
options.C: Stores stock sheet for the finished article
options.D: Advice of Internal Check issued by the Accounts office

e: The route card is the shop document showing the authority and sequence for manufacture of an article, produced to show how and under what instructions the manufacture was undertaken.

q: During cost compilation, the indirect expenses incurred inside one particular shop of a workshop are collected separately from the expenses common to the whole workshop. The expenses confined to that particular shop are termed:

options.A: Proforma on-cost of the workshop
options.B: Direct labour charges of the shop
options.C: Shop on-cost
options.D: Prime cost of the jobs done in the shop

e: Indirect expenses incurred inside and confined to one particular shop are shop on-cost, as distinct from general on-cost common to the whole workshop and proforma on-cost.

q: The salary of the general administrative and supervisory establishment that serves all the shops of a workshop together cannot be tied to any one shop. In workshop costing such indirect expenses common to the workshop as a whole form part of:

options.A: The direct material cost of jobs
options.B: The shop on-cost of the erecting shop alone
options.C: Proforma on-cost charged on capital jobs only
options.D: General on-cost

e: Salaries of general administrative and supervisory establishment serving all shops together form general on-cost, since they are indirect expenses common to the workshop as a whole.

q: In preparing the Workshop Manufacturing Suspense budget of a workshop, one credit head provided for is 'Issues to Stores'. This head represents:

options.A: Material manufactured in the workshop for stocking in stores depots
options.B: Stores purchased directly from the market during the year
options.C: Scrap expected to be sold through auction
options.D: Material returned by the shops to the depot as surplus

e: In the Workshop Manufacturing Suspense budget, Issues to Stores as a credit head represents material manufactured in the workshop for stocking in stores depots.

q: A manufacture job in a workshop has been completed and its final cost compiled. The amount accumulated under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense for that job is cleared by transfer to:

options.A: The Station Earnings account of the home station
options.B: Stores, Revenue or Capital heads, as applicable to the job
options.C: The Pension Fund of the railway
options.D: The shop on-cost account of the executing shop

e: On completion, the cost accumulated under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense for a job is cleared by transfer to Stores, Revenue or Capital heads, as applicable to that job.

q: The Workshop Accounts Officer is examining the monthly Workshop Outturn Statement and wants to see the expenditure incurred on the jobs of the shops. The part of the statement that shows this outlay is:

options.A: Part I of the Outturn Statement
options.B: The Plant Register abstract appended to the statement
options.C: Part II of the Outturn Statement
options.D: The stores issue summary appended to the statement

e: Part II of the monthly Workshop Outturn Statement shows the expenditure incurred on the jobs of the shops, while Part I deals with the outturn completed.

q: A shop incharge is asked to report, shop-wise, the work actually done and completed during the month for the Workshop Outturn Statement. This information about outturn is shown in:

options.A: Part II of the Outturn Statement
options.B: The Workshop General Register only
options.C: The labour pay sheet summary
options.D: Part I of the Outturn Statement

e: Part I of the Workshop Outturn Statement shows, shop-wise, the work actually done and completed during the month, that is, the outturn of each shop.

q: Under the system of job costing followed in a railway workshop, the expenditure on a manufacture or repair job is accumulated:

options.A: Separately for each job under its work order, covering labour, material and on-cost
options.B: In one pooled account for all jobs taken up during the year
options.C: Only in respect of material, labour being recorded shop-wise in total
options.D: Shop-wise in total, without any job-wise accumulation

e: Under job costing, expenditure on each manufacture or repair job is accumulated separately under its own work order, covering labour, material and on-cost for that job alone.

q: Gate cards show the attendance of a workshop worker, but the Accounts office also needs to know how his working time was spent on the different jobs he handled. The time spent by the employee on individual jobs is recorded through:

options.A: Stores stock sheets maintained in the depot
options.B: Job cards for the respective jobs
options.C: Completion reports of jobs already closed
options.D: The route cards of jobs yet to be taken up

e: Time spent by a worker on individual jobs is recorded through job cards for the respective jobs, while gate cards only show his attendance at the workshop.

q: Stores material is issued from the depot for execution of a workshop job covered by a work order. At the time of issue, the value of that material is initially debited to:

options.A: The final Revenue head of the job directly
options.B: The Stock Adjustment Account of the depot
options.C: Workshop Manufacturing Suspense, under the respective work order
options.D: The shop on-cost account of the receiving shop

e: Stores material issued for a workshop job is initially debited to Workshop Manufacturing Suspense under the respective work order, not directly to the final head or on-cost.

q: Owing to a power failure, workshop staff remain idle for some hours and the idle time cannot be charged to any job in hand. The wages paid for that idle time are charged to:

options.A: The capital work order of the shop concerned
options.B: The Pension Fund of the railway
options.C: The next job taken up by the staff after the failure
options.D: Shop on-cost

e: Wages for idle time caused by power failure, which cannot be charged to any job in hand, are charged to shop on-cost of the shop concerned.

q: The Workshop Accounts Office needs, for any job in hand, the work order under which it is running, the expenditure booked on it so far and the outturn already transferred. The register maintained primarily for recording these job-wise details is the:

options.A: Workshop General Register
options.B: Stores price ledger maintained for depot stock
options.C: Gate attendance register of the workshop
options.D: Muster roll kept for casual labour

e: The Workshop General Register records job-wise details for each job in hand: its work order, expenditure booked so far and outturn already transferred against it.

q: At the monthly reconciliation, the total cost of jobs in progress as worked out from the Workshop General Register is compared with the general books. It should agree with:

options.A: The balance under Stores Suspense in the general books
options.B: The balance under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense in the general books
options.C: The balance under Traffic Suspense in the general books
options.D: The total of the shop on-cost accounts for the month

e: The total cost of jobs in progress from the Workshop General Register must agree with the balance under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense in the general books, ensuring cost and financial accounts tally.

q: The Workshop Accounts Officer periodically reviews the Workshop General Register of the workshop. The main object of this review is to:

options.A: Fix the pay of the staff working on the outstanding jobs
options.B: Verify the cash balance held in the workshop cash office
options.C: Detect jobs lying incomplete or outstanding for long periods and secure their early clearance
options.D: Prepare the annual stores budget of the railway

e: Periodic review of the Workshop General Register aims to detect jobs lying incomplete or outstanding for long periods and to secure their early completion and clearance.

q: Components manufactured in a workshop are ready to be taken into the stock of the stores depot. The value at which such manufactured articles are taken into stores stock is:

options.A: The prevailing market price of similar articles
options.B: Direct material cost only, excluding labour and on-cost
options.C: A fixed rate notified for all workshops irrespective of cost
options.D: Cost of manufacture, that is, material, labour and on-cost

e: Components manufactured for stores stock are taken into stock at cost of manufacture, that is, material plus labour plus on-cost, not at market price or material cost alone.

q: During an overhaul job, serviceable released material and scrap arise and are assessed. The value of scrap and released material arising from that job is dealt with by:

options.A: Crediting it to the job under its work order at its assessed value
options.B: Debiting it to the job as an additional material cost
options.C: Crediting it to the Pension Fund of the railway
options.D: Allowing the shop incharge to sell it directly from the shop

e: Scrap and serviceable released material arising from a job are credited to that job under its work order at assessed value, reducing the net cost borne by the job.

q: Material was drawn for a job but a part of it is found surplus and is returned to the stores depot. The accounting treatment of the returned material is to:

options.A: Debit its value again to Workshop Manufacturing Suspense
options.B: Credit its value to the work order from which it was drawn
options.C: Write off its value to shop on-cost of the shop
options.D: Treat its value as proceeds of scrap sale

e: Material drawn for a job but returned surplus to the stores depot is credited to the work order from which it was drawn, so the job bears only the material actually consumed.

q: A workshop completes a job executed for the use of its own railway and the cost is to be transferred to the final head. Such jobs for the home railway are transferred:

options.A: At market rates with an element of profit added
options.B: At rates fixed by the Comptroller and Auditor General
options.C: At cost, without any profit element
options.D: At cost plus ten per cent as departmental profit

e: Jobs executed for the home railway are transferred at cost, without any profit element, as they are departmental work and not a commercial sale to an outside party.

q: The Accounts office does not wait for the actual indirect expenses of a month before charging on-cost to jobs completed in that month. On-cost is charged to jobs at rates which are:

options.A: Decided by each shop incharge from month to month
options.B: Always equal to the material cost of the job
options.C: Notified in the Stores Code for all workshops
options.D: Predetermined on the basis of anticipated indirect expenses and anticipated direct labour

e: On-cost is charged at predetermined rates based on anticipated indirect expenses and anticipated direct labour, so job costs need not wait for actual expenses of the month.

q: The general on-cost collected for a workshop as a whole has to be shared among its shops before it is charged to jobs. This apportionment among the shops is generally made on the basis of:

options.A: Direct labour charges of each shop
options.B: Floor area occupied by each shop
options.C: Number of machines installed in each shop
options.D: Number of staff borne on the rolls of each shop

e: General on-cost collected for the workshop as a whole is apportioned among shops generally on the basis of direct labour charges of each shop before charging it to jobs.

q: A direct worker avails authorised leave and his wages for the leave period cannot be booked to any particular job handled by him. Such leave wages are charged to:

options.A: A capital work order of the shop
options.B: Shop on-cost
options.C: Stores Suspense pending his return from leave
options.D: The next job undertaken by him on return

e: Leave wages of a direct worker for authorised leave cannot be booked to any particular job, so they are charged to shop on-cost as an indirect charge of that shop.

q:
Consider the following statements about overtime wages in a workshop:
1. Overtime wages paid for a specific urgent job are charged to that job.
2. Overtime wages not attributable to any specific job are charged to on-cost.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Overtime for a specific urgent job is charged to that job, while overtime not attributable to any specific job is charged to on-cost. Both statements are therefore correct.

q: A machine belonging to a shop undergoes ordinary repairs and maintenance carried out within the workshop. The cost of such ordinary repairs to the shop's own machinery and plant is charged to:

options.A: The Capital head of the workshop
options.B: The job that happened to be running on the machine
options.C: Stores Suspense of the attached depot
options.D: Shop on-cost

e: Cost of ordinary repairs and maintenance of a shop's own machinery and plant, done within the workshop, is charged to shop on-cost and not to Capital or to a running job.

q: Workers in a shop earn bonus under the incentive scheme for time saved on jobs. In workshop accounts, the bonus so earned is accounted for as:

options.A: Part of the labour cost, charged to the respective jobs or work orders
options.B: A charge to the Staff Benefit Fund of the railway
options.C: General on-cost in all cases, irrespective of the jobs done
options.D: A deduction from the material cost of the jobs concerned

e: Incentive bonus earned for time saved is part of labour cost and is charged to the respective jobs or work orders on which the time was saved.

q: A work order is opened in a workshop for one particular identified manufacture job and is closed when that job is finished. Such an order is a specific work order, which differs from a standing work order in that a standing work order:

options.A: Is issued only by the Railway Board for capital jobs
options.B: Covers routine repetitive work, whereas the specific order is for a particular identified job
options.C: Is never closed even after the work is completed
options.D: Is valid only for work done for other railways

e: A standing work order covers routine repetitive work over a period, whereas a specific work order is issued for one particular identified job and closed when that job is finished.

q: Standard components are manufactured in a workshop in lots for stocking in the stores depot, and the cost is accumulated for the lot as a whole rather than article by article. Such manufacture is executed under:

options.A: Batch work orders
options.B: Revenue standing work orders only
options.C: Verbal instructions of the shop incharge
options.D: Material requisitions without any work order

e: Standard components manufactured in lots for stores stock, with cost accumulated for the lot as a whole, are executed under batch work orders.

q: A work order issued for a workshop job is examined in the Accounts office to see whether it is complete in a vital respect. Every work order must invariably indicate:

options.A: The name of the worker who will execute the job
options.B: The head of account or allocation to which the cost of the job is chargeable
options.C: The market price expected for the finished article
options.D: The date on which the next overhaul of the workshop falls due

e: Every work order must invariably indicate the head of account or allocation to which the cost of the job is chargeable, so expenditure is booked to the correct final head.

q: A workshop job has been completed, its cost transferred out and its work order closed. Thereafter, a further charge is sought to be booked to the same work order. The correct position is that:

options.A: Material charges alone may still be booked to it till the year ends
options.B: Labour charges alone may still be booked to it till the year ends
options.C: No further expenditure can be booked to that closed work order
options.D: Charges may be booked to it till the next job in the shop is completed

e: Once a job is completed, its cost transferred and its work order closed, no further expenditure of any kind can be booked to that closed work order.

q: Material is issued from the stores depot to a workshop job and its value has to be debited to the work order. The rate applied for pricing this issue is:

options.A: The latest market rate ruling on the date of issue
options.B: A rate fixed by the shop incharge receiving the material
options.C: The rate at which the material was originally manufactured
options.D: The stores price-ledger issue rate

e: Material issued from the stores depot to a work order is priced at the stores price-ledger issue rate, the authorised rate for valuing stores issues.

q: On completion of a workshop job, the executive prepares a completion report for the job. The purpose of this report is to:

options.A: Record the final cost of the job and compare it with the sanctioned estimate
options.B: Fix the pay of the staff who worked on the job
options.C: Close the accounts of the workshop for the month
options.D: Revise the rates in the stores price ledger

e: The completion report records the final cost of a completed job and compares it with the sanctioned estimate, to reveal excess or saving and close the work order.

q: The labour pay sheets for workshop staff for a month are under preparation. These pay sheets are prepared by:

options.A: The shop incharge from the route cards of completed jobs
options.B: The Accounts office from the time and tally sheets rendered by the shops
options.C: The Personnel Branch from the leave records of the staff
options.D: The Cash office from the gate attendance register

e: Labour pay sheets are prepared by the Accounts office from the time and tally sheets rendered by the shops, which show attendance and time booked to jobs.

q: Before a job is brought under the incentive scheme, an allowed time has to be set for it. The allowed time for a job is fixed on the basis of:

options.A: Negotiation with the recognised union of the workshop
options.B: The actual time taken on the same job in the previous year
options.C: Time studies and work measurement carried out by the rate fixer
options.D: A rough estimate given by the shop incharge

e: Allowed time for a job brought under incentive is fixed on the basis of time studies and work measurement by the rate fixer, not by negotiation or past actual time.

q: Under the Group Incentive Scheme in a repair workshop, a group turns out some units, of which a part is rejected on inspection. Incentive under the scheme is computed on the basis of:

options.A: All outturn produced, including the rejected work
options.B: Attendance of the members of the group during the period
options.C: Savings in the cost of material achieved by the group
options.D: Only such outturn as is passed and accepted

e: Under the Group Incentive Scheme, incentive is computed only on outturn passed and accepted at inspection. Rejected outturn is excluded from the computation.

q:
Consider the following statements about machinery provided under the Machinery and Plant Programme:
1. The cost of additional new machinery under the programme is charged to Capital.
2. The cost of replacement of existing machinery under the programme is charged to the Depreciation Reserve Fund.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Under the Machinery and Plant Programme, cost of additional new machinery is charged to Capital and cost of replacement of existing machinery to the Depreciation Reserve Fund, so both statements are correct.

q: Expenditure has been booked under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense on jobs that remain incomplete at the close of the financial year. This expenditure represents:

options.A: A loss to be written off within the same financial year
options.B: Work-in-progress, carried forward under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense to the next year
options.C: Revenue earnings of the workshop for the year
options.D: Dead surplus stock lying in the workshop

e: Expenditure on incomplete jobs at year-end is work-in-progress and is carried forward under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense to the next year, not written off as a loss.

q: The cost sheet of a manufactured article already shows prime cost together with shop on-cost and general on-cost. The full cost of the article is arrived at by adding to that total:

options.A: Direct labour cost alone
options.B: Direct material cost alone
options.C: Proforma on-cost
options.D: The selling price expected for the article

e: Full cost is prime cost plus shop on-cost and general on-cost plus proforma on-cost. The proforma element is added last to make the cost comparable with trade cost.

q: For a workshop job, prime cost has been compiled from the charges booked under its work order. The works cost, also called shop cost, of the job is obtained as:

options.A: Prime cost plus general on-cost and proforma on-cost together
options.B: Direct material cost alone
options.C: Prime cost plus proforma on-cost alone
options.D: Prime cost plus shop on-cost

e: Works cost, also called shop cost, is prime cost plus shop on-cost. General and proforma on-cost are added later to arrive at the full cost of the job.

q: A chargeman asks which elements make up the prime cost of a job in the workshop cost sheet. The prime cost of a workshop job consists of:

options.A: Direct material and shop on-cost only
options.B: Direct labour and general on-cost only
options.C: Direct material, direct labour and direct expenses chargeable to the job
options.D: All costs of the job including proforma on-cost

e: Prime cost consists only of direct material, direct labour and direct expenses chargeable to the job. On-cost elements are excluded from prime cost.

q: On-cost was absorbed on jobs during a period at predetermined rates, and at the end of the period the absorbed amount is compared with the actual on-cost incurred. The difference between the two is known as:

options.A: Work-in-progress of the workshop
options.B: The suspense balance of the workshop
options.C: Departmental charges of the workshop
options.D: Over-absorption or under-absorption of on-cost

e: The difference between on-cost absorbed at predetermined rates and actual on-cost incurred is over-absorption if absorbed is more, and under-absorption if it is less.

q: A shop has incurred a known total of shop on-cost and its total direct labour charges for the period are also known. The shop on-cost percentage applied to jobs of that shop is worked out as:

options.A: Total direct labour divided by total shop on-cost, expressed as a percentage
options.B: Total shop on-cost divided by total material cost of the shop
options.C: Total shop on-cost divided by the number of jobs done in the shop
options.D: Total shop on-cost divided by total direct labour charges of the shop, expressed as a percentage

e: Shop on-cost percentage is total shop on-cost divided by total direct labour charges of the shop, expressed as a percentage, for absorption on a direct labour basis.

q: While evaluating a proposal to buy a new machine for a shop, the Workshop Accounts Officer insists that the comparison should not stop at the purchase price. In life-cycle costing of a workshop machine, the cost considered over the whole life of the machine comprises:

options.A: Only the maintenance cost incurred after the machine is installed
options.B: The acquisition cost together with the operating, maintenance and disposal costs over its life
options.C: Only the purchase price paid for the machine at the time of its acquisition
options.D: Only the depreciation charged on the machine in its first year of use

e: Life-cycle costing considers the whole-life cost of a machine: acquisition cost plus operating, maintenance and disposal costs over its life, not purchase price alone.

q: A shop is told the price at which a component will be acceptable and the margin expected on it, and is asked to work backwards to the cost it must not exceed. Under target costing, the allowable cost of the component is arrived at by:

options.A: Deducting the desired margin from the price at which the component is expected to be acceptable
options.B: Adding a desired margin to the cost actually incurred on the component
options.C: Taking the cost of the same component in the previous period, without any change
options.D: Averaging the costs quoted by different shops for the component

e: Under target costing, allowable cost is the acceptable or target price minus the desired margin. The shop must produce within that cost worked backwards from price.

q: To keep stores holding and work-in-progress low, a workshop arranges supplies so that material reaches the shop only when the work in hand actually calls for it. Such a just-in-time arrangement means that the material is arranged to reach the shop:

options.A: In one large lot covering the requirement of a long period, well in advance
options.B: Only after the job for which it is required has been completed
options.C: As and when it is actually needed for the work in hand, so that the stock and work-in-progress held are kept low
options.D: Through the personal custody of the worker executing the job

e: Just-in-time means material is arranged to reach the shop as and when actually needed for work in hand, keeping stores holding and work-in-progress low.

q: The same stores item is being described by different names in different shops, causing confusion in accountal. Codification of the items of material used in a workshop and its stores consists of:

options.A: Arranging the items in the bins of the depot in order of their size
options.B: Recording the name of the supplier against each item in the ledger
options.C: Marking the price of each item on the bin in which it is stocked
options.D: Allotting a systematic code to each item so that it can be identified and accounted for uniformly

e: Codification means allotting a systematic code to each stores item so it can be identified and accounted for uniformly in all shops and depots, avoiding confusion of names.

q: The stores attached to a workshop classify their holdings for the FSN analysis before a stock review. Under FSN analysis, the items are classified according to:

options.A: The speed at which they move or are consumed, as fast-moving, slow-moving or non-moving items
options.B: The value of each item held in stock
options.C: The country from which each item was procured
options.D: The size and weight of each item in the stock

e: FSN analysis classifies stores items by speed of movement or consumption as fast-moving, slow-moving and non-moving, for stock review and control.

q: At the close of a period, the workshop prepares a manufacturing account for the work done in its shops. Such a manufacturing account is intended mainly to ascertain:

options.A: The profit earned by the workshop on the work done for outside parties
options.B: The cost of production of the outturn completed during the period
options.C: The amount outstanding against other railways at the close of the period
options.D: The wages payable to the staff of the workshop for the period

e: A manufacturing account is prepared to ascertain the cost of production of the outturn completed during the period, from material, labour and on-cost consumed.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A cash discount obtained from a supplier on a purchase is treated in the cost accounts as a financial receipt, and the material continues to be costed without deducting the discount from it.
2. Interest on the capital locked up in the workshop is always loaded on jobs as an element of their cost.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Cash discount is a financial receipt and material is costed without deducting it, so statement 1 is correct. Interest on capital is not loaded on jobs, so statement 2 is wrong.

q: A manufacture estimate prepared by the executive of a workshop is put up for sanction. Before it is sanctioned by the competent authority, the estimate is:

options.A: Approved by the stores depot attached to the workshop
options.B: Sent to the Railway Board in all cases, irrespective of its value
options.C: Certified by the Production Control Organisation alone
options.D: Vetted by the Workshop Accounts Office as associated finance

e: A manufacture estimate is vetted by the Workshop Accounts Office as associated finance before sanction by the competent authority, to check rates, allocation and funds.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Before the balance under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense is carried into the next year, it is checked against the jobs physically in progress, so that only genuine work-in-progress is carried forward.
2. Once the annual accounts are closed, the balance under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense is carried forward exactly as it stands, with no check of the jobs in progress.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 2 only
options.B: 1 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Before carry-forward, the Workshop Manufacturing Suspense balance is checked against jobs physically in progress so only genuine work-in-progress is carried forward. Statement 1 alone is correct.

q: Articles turned out by a shop are rejected for bad workmanship and have to be put right. The cost of rectifying such articles is accounted for:

options.A: As a normal addition to the cost of the original job
options.B: As a recovery from the Provident Fund of the worker concerned
options.C: As cost of defective work charged to the shop on-cost, so that the legitimate cost of the job is not inflated
options.D: As capital expenditure of the workshop

e: Cost of rectifying articles rejected for bad workmanship is charged as defective work to shop on-cost, so the legitimate cost of the original job is not inflated.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Day-to-day running repairs and examination of rolling stock are carried out at open-line depots such as loco sheds and carriage and wagon depots.
2. Periodic Overhaul and heavy repairs of rolling stock are carried out in workshops.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Day-to-day running repairs and examination are done at open-line depots like loco sheds and carriage and wagon depots, while Periodic Overhaul and heavy repairs are done in workshops. Both are correct.

q: A shop asks whether its machines should be attended to only when they break down. The maintenance of the machinery and plant of a workshop itself is carried out:

options.A: Only when a machine breaks down completely
options.B: Only by the manufacturers of the machines
options.C: Only at the time of the annual accounts closing
options.D: In accordance with planned maintenance schedules, in addition to repairs of breakdowns as they occur

e: Workshop machinery and plant are maintained to planned maintenance schedules, in addition to attending to breakdown repairs as they occur, not only after complete breakdown.

q: Cranes and traversers move material about the workshop and serve the shops generally, not any one job. The cost of such internal transport of material within the workshop is treated as:

options.A: A direct charge on the job for which material was last moved
options.B: General on-cost of the workshop
options.C: A charge to the Capital head of the workshop
options.D: A deduction from the material cost of jobs

e: Cost of internal transport by cranes and traversers serving shops generally, and not any one job, is treated as general on-cost of the workshop.

q: A consignment is bought specially for one manufacture job and freight and carriage are paid on it by the workshop. Such freight and carriage is:

options.A: Charged to general on-cost of the workshop
options.B: Charged to the stores depot as its handling expense
options.C: Charged to that job as a direct expense, forming part of its prime cost
options.D: Recovered from the supplier in all cases

e: Freight and carriage paid on a consignment bought specially for one job is a direct expense of that job and forms part of its prime cost.

q: In a carriage workshop, the bogies taken out from under coaches and wagons under overhaul are attended to in the section of the workshop known as the:

options.A: Bogie shop
options.B: Foundry
options.C: Smithy
options.D: Upholstery shop

e: Bogies removed from coaches and wagons under overhaul are attended to in the bogie shop, the section specialising in bogie work in a carriage workshop.

q: The tool room and the power house serve all the production shops of a workshop and execute no saleable outturn of their own. The cost of such service shops is brought into the cost of jobs by:

options.A: Charging it directly to the first job taken up in the year
options.B: First apportioning it among the production shops served, whose on-cost is then absorbed on their jobs
options.C: Debiting it to Stores Suspense
options.D: Writing it off to revenue at the end of the year

e: Cost of service shops like the tool room and power house is first apportioned among the production shops served, and then absorbed on their jobs through their on-cost.

q: A clerk collects the on-cost of a shop for a period and then spreads it over the individual jobs done in that shop. In workshop costing, this process of charging the on-cost of a shop to its individual jobs is known as:

options.A: Allocation of on-cost
options.B: Apportionment of on-cost
options.C: Absorption of on-cost
options.D: Accumulation of on-cost

e: Charging the collected on-cost of a shop to its individual jobs is absorption of on-cost, distinct from allocation to one centre or apportionment between centres.

q: Job costs in a workshop are charged with on-cost at predetermined rates instead of waiting for the actual indirect expenses of the period to be collected. This is done mainly so that:

options.A: The actual on-cost need never be ascertained at all
options.B: The shops can fix their own rates without any basis
options.C: On-cost can be charged at double the actual amount
options.D: Job costs can be compiled and the outturn transferred promptly, without waiting for the actual indirect expenses of the period to be collected

e: Predetermined on-cost rates allow job costs to be compiled and outturn transferred promptly, without waiting for actual indirect expenses of the period to be collected.

q: For collecting and controlling costs, the accounts of a workshop do not treat the workshop as one undifferentiated whole. For this purpose, each shop or section of the workshop is treated as a:

options.A: Cost centre
options.B: Profit centre
options.C: Stores depot
options.D: Separate accounting unit rendering its own Account Current

e: For collecting and controlling costs, each shop or section is treated as a cost centre, with its expenses accumulated separately for absorption on its jobs.

q: Before a manufacture job is taken in hand, the planning office issues a material schedule for it. A 'bill of materials' prepared for a manufacture job in a workshop shows:

options.A: The wages payable to the workers on the job
options.B: All the materials, with their quantities, required for the execution of the job
options.C: The machines required for the job
options.D: The on-cost percentage applicable to the job

e: A bill of materials for a manufacture job lists all materials, with quantities, required for execution of the job, forming the basis for indenting and issue.

q: Worn-out components of rolling stock are built up and machined back to size in a workshop where doing so is economical, instead of being replaced by new ones. Such work is known as:

options.A: Condemnation of components
options.B: Cannibalisation of components
options.C: Reclamation of components
options.D: Standardisation of components

e: Building up worn-out components and machining them back to size, where economical, instead of replacing them with new ones, is reclamation of components.

q: A large manufacture job is spread over several shops, each shop making a part of it. Components of such a job produced in different shops are executed under:

options.A: Revenue standing work orders
options.B: A separate sanctioned estimate for each component
options.C: The personal account of the shop incharge
options.D: Sub-work orders opened under the main work order, their costs being consolidated under the main work order

e: Components of a large job spread over several shops are executed under sub-work orders opened under the main work order, their costs being consolidated under the main order.

q: Before the shop on-cost of a period can be spread over jobs, it is first collected at one place. Before being apportioned to jobs, the shop on-cost of a workshop is first collected:

options.A: Under separate on-cost (standing) work orders maintained for the shop
options.B: Directly in the Balance Sheet of the railway
options.C: In the Stores Suspense account
options.D: Through the contractor's ledger

e: Shop on-cost is first collected under separate on-cost standing work orders maintained for the shop, before being apportioned and absorbed on jobs of that shop.

q: A new time keeper is told that his work at the gate is not the same as the time booking done in the shops. 'Time keeping', as distinct from 'time booking', in a workshop refers to:

options.A: Recording the time spent by a worker on each job
options.B: Recording the attendance of workers, i.e., their time of arrival at and departure from the workshop
options.C: Fixing the allowed time for a job
options.D: Preparing the labour pay sheets of the shop

e: Time keeping means recording attendance, that is, arrival and departure of workers at the workshop. Recording time spent on each job is time booking, a separate function.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. With a rise in the volume of outturn of a workshop, the fixed on-cost borne by each unit of outturn comes down.
2. The variable on-cost borne by each unit of outturn stays broadly the same when the volume of outturn changes.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Fixed on-cost per unit falls as outturn volume rises, while variable on-cost per unit stays broadly the same with change in volume. Both statements are therefore correct.
